kurals.tamil:
கரப்பினுங் கையிகந் தொல்லாநின் உண்கண்
உரைக்கல் உறுவதொன் றுண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Karappinung kaiyikan thollaanin unkan
uraikkal uruvadhon rundu.
kurals.meaning: Even though you try to hide it, your darkened eyes refuse to be held back; there is something they are trying to tell me.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend who says ‘I’m fine’ but whose eyes look sad. You can tell something is wrong, because eyes often say what words keep hidden. The poet says love works the same way: the eyes give away the secret.
kurals.university: The chapter title kuṟippaṟivuṟuttal means ‘making known by signs’ (kuṟippu, a hint or covert sign; aṟivuṟuttal, causing to be known), and it belongs to the kaṟpu (wedded love) section, where partners communicate feelings about separation without open speech. Here the husband addresses his wife: karappiṉum (‘though you hide it’), her uṇkaṇ (eyes darkened with collyrium) kai ikantu ollā (‘will not stay within bounds’) and are about to utter (uraikkal uṟuvatu) one thing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as a message the eyes force past her concealment; Solomon Pappaiah stresses the painted eyes; Kalaignar names the hidden message as a love that does not want separation, which fits the chapter’s setting of an impending departure. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi as கையிகந் தொல்லாநின்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s play, King Dushyanta notes that Shakuntala does not join her words to his, yet she listens when he speaks, and though she does not turn her face to him, her eyes rest on nothing else for long.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala is too modest to speak her love, but her eyes betray it, and the king reads them.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe a woman whose speech hides her heart while her eyes give it away to the one who loves her.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known stanza from Act 1; a close match on eyes revealing concealed love, though the context is first love rather than a married couple facing separation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that what people keep hidden will in the end come to light.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the same principle to a lover’s heart: what she hides, her eyes reveal.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the idea that concealment fails, but Luke speaks of hypocrisy exposed, not love betrayed by the eyes.

islam.quote_or_event: “He knows that which deceives the eyes and what the breasts conceal.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God knows both the stolen glance and the secret held in the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural links the same two things, hidden feeling in the heart and its leak through the eyes, though here it is the husband, not God, who reads them.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a real pairing of eyes and concealed hearts, but the verse concerns divine omniscience and misused glances, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my bride; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one bead of thy necklace.”
judaism.explanation: The lover in the Song says a single glance from his bride is enough to capture him.
judaism.tie_back: In both poems the beloved’s eyes speak with a force that needs no words.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a strong match on the eyes’ power in love, though the Song praises the glance rather than describing a hidden message.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists three things that are carried on in secret and three that shine openly, the sun, the moon and the Dhamma, which need no concealment.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta contrasts what must hide from view with what is naturally open and shining.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows a secret that cannot stay hidden; the sutta’s contrast between the concealed and the openly shining is the nearest Buddhist parallel, though its concern is truth, not love.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a real short sutta; only a loose next-best link on hiddenness versus disclosure, with no reference to eyes or love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the assembly he pronounces holy (words), yet secretly he commits sins; but the wise know him to be a deceiver and great rogue.”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga observes that a monk who hides his lapses behind pious words is still seen through by the discerning.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, concealment fails before someone who knows how to read the signs, though the Jain text is exposing hypocrisy, not tender feeling.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares only the idea that hidden things are perceived by the discerning, in a monastic warning context very different from the Kural’s.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Medea first sees Jason in the palace of Aeetes, she keeps stealing glances at him, and her eyes and blushing cheeks betray the love she is struggling to hide from her family.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows a young woman’s secret passion leaking out through her gaze despite her efforts to keep it silent.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Medea’s eyes, like the wife’s in the Kural, refuse to keep the heart’s secret.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a good match on eyes betraying hidden love, though it is first love rather than a married couple’s unspoken grief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Emerson writes that the eyes of men converse at least as much as their tongues, and that this ocular dialect needs no dictionary but is understood all the world over.
philosophy.explanation: Emerson treats the eye as a language of its own that communicates even when speech is guarded.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s whole point is that the eyes speak a message the tongue holds back.
philosophy.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Conduct of Life, ‘Behavior’ (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong thematic match on the eyes as a wordless language, though Emerson writes generally about manners, not love.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணிறைந்த காரிகைக் காம்பேர்தோட் பேதைக்குப்
பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை பெரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Kanniraindha kaarikaik kaamperdhot pedhaikkup
penniraindha neermai peridhu.
kurals.meaning: My innocent beloved, whose beauty fills my eyes and whose shoulders are like bamboo, has a womanly modesty even greater than her beauty.
kurals.elementary: Some people are beautiful to look at, but what makes them special is how gentle and kind they are. The poet says his beloved is lovely, but her quiet, modest nature is even bigger than her beauty.
kurals.university: The speaker praises the heroine’s kārikai (beauty) that fills the eye (kaṇ niṟainta) and her shoulders like the bamboo (kāmpu ēr tōḷ), a stock Tamil image of smooth, rounded grace; pētai here means an artless, innocent young woman. Her peṇ niṟainta nīrmai (‘a nature full of womanliness’) is said to be peritu, very great. Commentators gloss peṇmai variously: Mu. Varadarasanar as the quality of womanhood, Solomon Pappaiah as an excellence surpassing that found in all women, and Kalaignar as womanliness that is itself her greatest beauty. In the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, the speaker is the husband telling the confidante (tōḻi) that his wife’s modesty is so great that she cannot voice her own feelings, which is why they must be read through signs. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Parvati comes before Shiva and his composure stirs, she betrays her own feeling only through her trembling limbs and stands with her lovely face turned aside, too shy to speak.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa portrays Parvati’s love as visible in her bashful bearing rather than in any words.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Parvati is beautiful but her modesty is what governs how her love can be expressed.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; matches the pairing of beauty with modest, wordless feeling, but Kalidasa praises a goddess, not a wife’s character above her looks.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: The apostle ranks a gentle, quiet spirit above outward beauty and adornment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the beloved’s modest nature is greater than the beauty that fills the eye.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on inner modesty outranking beauty, though the epistle gives moral instruction rather than a lover’s praise.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then one of the two women came to him walking with shyness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an notes the modest bearing of the daughter of Madyan who came to invite Moses to her father’s house.
islam.tie_back: The Kural, too, singles out a young woman’s shyness as her most notable quality.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a genuine image of praised feminine modesty, though the verse is narrative and not a lover’s praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.”
judaism.explanation: The poem of the woman of valour ends by placing character above charm and beauty.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker reaches the same verdict: her womanly nature is greater than her looks.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); good match on inner quality over beauty, though Proverbs dismisses beauty while the Kural also delights in it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Queen Mallika asks the Buddha why some women are beautiful and others plain, and he explains that outward appearance follows from inner qualities such as freedom from anger.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta ties a woman’s beauty to her character rather than treating it as independent of it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also looks past beauty to the womanly nature beneath it, though without any teaching on karma.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a real sutta; a partial link between beauty and inner disposition, but the Buddhist frame is karmic cause, not a lover’s praise of modesty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Now this daughter of an excellent king was virtuous and well looking; she possessed all lucky marks of the body, and shone forth like the lightning Saudâmanî.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana introduces Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, by naming her virtue before her beauty.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the bride is beautiful, but her virtue comes first.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a real Jain portrait of a virtuous, beautiful bride, though it is a brief description rather than praise of modesty above beauty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, meeting Nausicaa on the shore, compares her to a young palm shoot he once saw springing up beside Apollo’s altar on Delos, and speaks to her with awe.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures a modest young woman’s grace through a slender growing plant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s bamboo shoulders and Odysseus’s palm sapling are parallel plant images for a modest girl’s beauty.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.160-169 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous simile; the plant image and modest maiden match well, though Odysseus is a stranger flattering her, not a lover.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diotima teaches that the lover should come to value beauty of soul above beauty of the body.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s ladder of love moves from bodily beauty toward the higher beauty of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s speaker makes the same move, praising her nature as greater than her looks.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 210b-c (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a reasonable match on inner beauty outranking outer, though Plato’s ascent is philosophical, not marital.

kurals.tamil:
மணியில் திகழ்தரு நூல்போல் மடந்தை
அணியில் திகழ்வதொன்று உண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Maniyil thikazhdharu noolpol madandhai
aniyil thikazhvadhondru undu.
kurals.meaning: Just as the thread shows through the crystal beads strung on it, something shines through this young woman’s beauty.
kurals.elementary: If you thread clear glass beads on a string, you can see the string running through them. The poet says his beloved’s beauty is like those beads: you can see a hidden feeling running through it, if you look closely.
kurals.university: The image is of a string of maṇi (gems or crystal beads) through which the nūl (thread) can be seen; the maṭantai (young woman) has something that likewise tikaḻvatu, shines through her aṇi (beauty or adornment). Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss that ‘something’ as a kuṟippu, a hidden intent visible within her beauty; Solomon Pappaiah takes the gems as clear crystal (paḷiṅku) through which the thread is seen, and Kalaignar as a sign that enchants the speaker. In the traditional arrangement the husband speaks to the confidante, saying the wife’s hidden feeling is legible through her looks. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the thread-and-gem simile is also famous from Bhagavad Gita 7.7, though there it describes the divine as the string on which the world is threaded.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O conqueror of wealth, there is no truth superior to Me. Everything rests upon Me, as pearls are strung on a thread.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says he is the hidden thread holding all things together, as a string holds a necklace of pearls.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same thread-through-gems image for a hidden meaning running through visible beauty.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 7.7 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; an exact match of image, but the Gita describes God as the support of the world, not a lover’s hidden feeling.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what is inside a person shows itself on the outside.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural sees the same movement from inside to outside, an inner feeling showing through her beauty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the principle that the inner shows through the outer, but in speech and moral terms rather than a lover’s look.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the inner devotion of the faithful leaves a visible sign on their faces.
islam.tie_back: As the thread shows through the beads, an inner state shows through the face in both texts.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a real case of inner disposition visible outwardly, but it concerns worship, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man’s wisdom maketh his face to shine, and the boldness of his face is changed.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes says inner wisdom becomes visible as a light in the face.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural also sees something inward shining through outward beauty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); matches the idea of inner quality shining outward, though wisdom rather than love is meant.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares the meditator’s insight to a man of good eyesight holding a clear, well-polished beryl gem through which a coloured thread runs, and seeing both the gem and the thread inside it.
buddhism.explanation: The simile describes seeing clearly how consciousness is bound up with the body, as a thread is seen through a gem.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the identical picture of a thread visible within a gem, but for a feeling seen within beauty.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known simile; the image is a near-exact match, but the subject is meditative insight, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A young woman, putting on fine ornaments and clothes, will say to a Sramana: ‘I shall give up (my former way of life) and practise the rough (viz. control). Reverend sir, teach me the Law!’”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that a woman’s ornaments and pious words may carry a hidden intention.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also sees an intention running beneath a woman’s adornment, but reads it tenderly where the Jain text reads it with suspicion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only a loose next-best link (a hidden aim beneath ornaments), in a renunciatory text whose wary view of women differs sharply from the Kural’s.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells how the gods adorned Pandora with a golden band, garlands and every grace, while Hermes placed within her a hidden nature of his own devising.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod the first woman’s adornment conceals something set inside her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural also sees something within a woman’s beauty, though for Valluvar it is a tender feeling, while for Hesiod it is guile.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 60-82 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; shares the structure of something hidden within adornment, but Hesiod’s view of women is hostile, so the fit is weak.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Alcibiades compares Socrates to the statues of Silenus sold in workshops, which open up to reveal images of the gods inside.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the image to say that something precious lies inside an outward form and can be seen by those who look within.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural also speaks of something within a visible form that shines out to the attentive eye.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 215a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous image; a good match on an inner treasure within an outer form, though Plato contrasts an ugly exterior with inner beauty.

kurals.tamil:
முகைமொக்குள் உள்ளது நாற்றம்போல் பேதை
நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன் றுண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Mukaimokkul ulladhu naatrampol pedhai
nakaimokkul ulladhon rundu.
kurals.meaning: As fragrance lies hidden inside an unopened bud, something lies hidden inside this innocent girl’s budding smile.
kurals.elementary: A flower bud doesn’t smell much yet, but the sweet smell is already inside, waiting. The poet says his beloved’s small smile is like that bud: it holds a feeling she hasn’t said out loud yet.
kurals.university: The couplet pairs two ‘buds’: mukai-mokkuḷ, the closed bud of a flower that holds its nāṟṟam (fragrance), and nakai-mokkuḷ, the bud of a smile, the half-formed smile of the pētai (innocent young woman), which holds ‘something’. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss that something as a kuṟippu, a hidden intent; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar make it explicit as her thoughts of her lover filling the smile. As in 1272-1273, the speaker is traditionally the husband addressing the confidante about signs he can read in the heroine. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; Pope’s rendering on ytamizh (‘budding smile of this dear damsel’s eyes’) adds the eyes, which are not in the Tamil.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Seeing Shakuntala, Dushyanta describes her lower lip as having the colour of a young leaf, her arms as tender shoots, and youth, alluring as a flower, as bound up in her limbs.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa describes a young woman’s beauty as a flower that has not yet fully opened.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same budding-flower image for a girl whose feeling is still folded within her smile.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known stanza; the flower-and-bud imagery of young love matches, but Kalidasa describes her body rather than a hidden meaning in her smile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land; The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give a good smell. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away.”
christianity.explanation: The Song pictures love as a spring of budding vines already giving off their fragrance.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, fragrance from unopened growth stands for love that is about to blossom.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good imagistic match on budding fragrance and love, though no smile or hidden meaning is mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith teaches that smiling in the face of one’s brother is an act of charity.
islam.explanation: The Prophet treats a smile as something that carries real meaning and value to the one who receives it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also treats a smile as carrying a message, though a lover’s rather than a charitable one.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, not re-verified this session; only a loose next-best match on the meaning a smile carries.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his precious fruits.”
judaism.explanation: The bride asks the winds to release the fragrance held within her garden for her beloved.
judaism.tie_back: In both poems a fragrance held within waits to be released to the beloved.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a close image of hidden fragrance and love, though the Song’s garden is not a smile.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color and also fragrant, even so, fruitful are the fair words of one who practices them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada distinguishes a flower that only looks beautiful from one that also carries fragrance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also prizes the fragrance inside the flower, the hidden meaning behind the visible smile.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; shares the image of fragrance as the inner substance of a flower, but applied to sincere speech, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Meekly and politely they approach him with their manifold arts to win his heart; and talking sweetly in confidential conversation they make him do (what they like).”
jainism.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that sweet manners and pleasant talk may carry a hidden purpose.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also reads a hidden meaning in a gentle outward sign, but with delight rather than the Jain monk’s caution.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a weak next-best match on gentle outward signs with an inner purpose, from a renunciatory text hostile to romance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that Aphrodite’s portion among gods and men includes the whispers of maidens and their smiles, along with sweet delight, love and gentleness.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod a maiden’s smile belongs to Aphrodite’s domain and carries love’s meaning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise finds love folded inside a girl’s smile.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 203-206 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a good match on the smile as love’s sign, though Hesiod also lists deceits among Aphrodite’s gifts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle distinguishes what exists only potentially from what exists actually, as the oak is present in the acorn before it grows.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, things can contain what they will become before it is visible.
philosophy.tie_back: The bud that already holds its scent, and the smile that already holds a feeling, are poetic cases of the potential within the actual.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a central doctrine; only a loose philosophical parallel to the bud image, with nothing about love; the acorn example is illustrative, not Aristotle’s own wording.

kurals.tamil:
செறிதொடி செய்திறந்த கள்ளம் உறுதுயர்
தீர்க்கும் மருந்தொன்று உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Seridhodi seydhirandha kallam urudhuyar
theerkkum marundhondru udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The secret sign that my beloved with her close-set bangles gave as she left holds a medicine that cures my deep sorrow.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a friend gives you a small wink or a smile that only you understand, and it makes you feel better right away. The poet says the secret look his beloved gave him was like medicine for his sadness.
kurals.university: The heroine is named by her ceṟi toṭi (closely set bangles), and what she did and left behind (ceytu iṟanta) is a kaḷḷam, a stealthy or covert sign. That sign holds one maruntu (medicine) that cures uṟu tuyar, great sorrow. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read kaḷḷam as a covert sign; Solomon Pappaiah stresses that it was shown so that only he would understand it; Kalaignar makes it her mischievous glance. The traditional reading has the husband, anxious about her reaction to his journey, comforted by a hidden sign of her consent or reassurance. Both sites give the same text; ytamizh’s English explanation (‘The well-meant departure of her whose bangles are tight-fitting...’) is a loose rendering of ceytu iṟanta, while Pope’s couplet calls the sign ‘secret wiles’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth canto, Krishna pleads with the offended Radha and begs her to place her tender foot on his head, calling that gesture the antidote that destroys the poison of love.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva makes a single gesture from the beloved the cure for the lover’s suffering.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural, too, finds the cure for great sorrow in one small sign from the beloved.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse (‘dehi pada-pallavam udaram’); a good match on the beloved’s gesture as medicine, though the setting is a lovers’ quarrel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride calls herself lovesick and asks for remedies to restore her.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat love’s sorrow as an illness needing a cure; in the Kural the cure is the beloved’s secret sign.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on love’s sickness and its remedy, though the remedy here is food, not a sign.

islam.quote_or_event: “Take this, my shirt, and cast it over the face of my father; he will become seeing.”
islam.explanation: Joseph sends his shirt as a token whose touch will heal his father’s grief-blinded eyes.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a token from the one longed for becomes the medicine for long sorrow.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a fitting image of a token that heals grief, though the love is between father and son.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says waiting sickens the heart, while a hope fulfilled restores life.
judaism.tie_back: The beloved’s sign in the Kural works the same way, turning sickening worry into healing reassurance.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); good match on longing as sickness and fulfilment as cure, though not about lovers specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Nanda pines for the beautiful Janapada Kalyani he left behind, the Buddha cures his longing by showing him the nymphs of the heavens, so that Nanda turns to the holy life.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats lovesickness as a malady and applies a skilful remedy to cure it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also speaks of a cure for love’s distress, but for Valluvar the cure is the beloved’s sign, while the Buddha’s cure leads away from her.
buddhism.source: Udana 3.2, Nanda Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a real sutta; matches only the idea of curing lovesickness, and the cure points in the opposite direction from the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Afterwards he will feel remorse like one who has drunk milk mixed with poison; considering the consequences, a worthy monk should have no intercourse with women.”
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monk, what seems sweet in a woman’s company is a poison disguised as milk.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural calls the beloved’s secret sign a medicine; the Jain text inverts the image, warning that such sweetness is poison for one seeking liberation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; used as an honest contrast, since Jain monastic teaching rejects the Kural’s view of a lover’s sign as healing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Helen puts into the wine a drug from Egypt that banishes grief and anger, so that whoever drinks it sheds no tear that day even for the dearest loss.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer imagines a medicine that dissolves sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s secret sign does what Helen’s drug does: it cures sorrow at once.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 4.219-226 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; matches the idea of a grief-curing medicine, but Helen’s is a literal drug, not a lover’s sign.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes the lover who finds in the beautiful beloved the only physician for his greatest pains.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus the beloved’s presence alone eases the anguish love produces.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the beloved’s sign the medicine for the lover’s sorrow, just as Plato makes the beloved the physician.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 252a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong match on the beloved as the only cure for love’s pain.

kurals.tamil:
பெரிதாற்றிப் பெட்பக் கலத்தல் அரிதாற்றி
அன்பின்மை சூழ்வ துடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Peridhaatrip petpak kalaththal aridhaatri
anpinmai soozhva thudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: His embracing me so lovingly and so intensely carries a hint that he is planning the hard parting again, and the lack of love it implies.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a parent who gives you an extra-long hug at the door, and you suddenly realise they are about to go on a trip. The heroine notices her husband’s extra-loving embrace and guesses that he is getting ready to leave her again.
kurals.university: The wife, speaking to her confidante, reads her husband’s unusually tender union (peritu āṟṟi, ‘showing great love’; peṭpak kalattal, ‘uniting so as to delight’) as a kuṟippu of something else: aritu āṟṟi, doing the hard thing, separation, and anpiṉmai cūḻvatu, contemplating lovelessness. Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it this way, as does Kalaignar, who says the embrace seems to signal another parting. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first half differently, as her having endured the past separation, so that his present embrace makes her think of his lack of love. Pope’s couplet on ytamizh (‘While lovingly embracing me, his heart is only grieved’) follows the separation reading. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rasa dance, when the gopis grow proud of Krishna’s attention after he has delighted them, he suddenly vanishes from among them, leaving them searching the forest for him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata shows an intense union with the beloved followed at once by his disappearance.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife fears exactly this pattern: closeness that signals an imminent departure.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.29-30 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; matches union followed by sudden separation, though Krishna’s disappearance has a devotional purpose the Kural does not share.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;”
christianity.explanation: Ecclesiastes says that embracing and parting each have their season.
christianity.tie_back: The wife in the Kural senses that a time of embracing is about to give way to a time apart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); only a general match on embrace and separation following each other, without the Kural’s reading of signs.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an addresses a wife who senses her husband drawing away and urges reconciliation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise detects signs of his withdrawal, though in her case through his very tenderness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); matches a wife’s fear of her husband’s distancing, but it is legal guidance and has no love poetry.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How canst thou say: I love thee, when thy heart is not with me?”
judaism.explanation: Delilah confronts Samson because his words of love do not match what she senses in his heart.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife also senses a gap between loving gestures and an intention to leave.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); matches the sense of love outwardly shown but inwardly withheld, though Delilah’s motive is betrayal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that attachment to the dear brings with it the fear of losing them.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife’s fear in the Kural, that even his embrace foretells parting, is the fear the Dhammapada says endearment produces.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; names the very fear the Kural shows, though the Buddhist answer is to give up attachment, not to read signs.

jainism.quote_or_event: On his wedding procession Arishtanemi turns back, renounces the world and leaves his bride Rajimati, who exclaims: ‘Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him!’
jainism.explanation: The Jain story centres on a bridegroom who leaves his bride at the very moment of union.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati suffers the departure that the Kural’s wife fears behind her husband’s embrace, though Arishtanemi leaves for renunciation, not for another journey.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.14-29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; Rajimati’s words at 22.29)
jainism._accuracy_note: Narrative summary checked against sacred-texts.com (Rajimati’s line is verbatim at 22.29); a partial match on a beloved departing at the moment of closeness, framed by Jainism as a spiritual victory.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Ariadne helps Theseus escape the Labyrinth and sails with him, he abandons her asleep on the island of Naxos.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth tells of a lover who leaves just after a time of closeness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife fears that her husband’s tender embrace is a prelude to such a leaving.
greek_mythology.source: Ariadne on Naxos, as told in Ovid, Heroides 10 and Catullus 64 (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth; matches abandonment after union, but Theseus’s desertion is a betrayal while the Kural’s husband leaves for duty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pausanias says the common lover, who loves the body rather than the soul, is not constant, and when the bloom fades he takes wing and flies away.
philosophy.explanation: Plato contrasts unstable love, which ends in departure, with lasting love of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife in the Kural fears that intensity of embrace may signal a love that is about to fly away.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; matches fear of love that will depart, though Plato’s concern is the quality of love, not a reading of signs.

kurals.tamil:
தண்ணந் துறைவன் தணந்தமை நம்மினும்
முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannan thuraivan thanandhamai namminum
munnam unarndha valai.
kurals.meaning: My bangles knew before I did that the lord of the cool shore had parted from me.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes your body knows you are sad before your mind does, like when you lose your appetite. The heroine says her arms grew so thin from missing her husband that her bangles slipped off, even before she understood he had left her in his heart.
kurals.university: The husband is called taṇṇam tuṟaivaṉ, ‘lord of the cool shore’, the conventional epithet of the hero of the neytal (seashore) landscape, whose mood in classical Tamil poetics is anxious waiting. His taṇantamai (having parted) was sensed by her vaḷai (bangles) even before (muṉṉam) by herself. The image rests on a classical convention: grief at separation makes the wife’s arms grow thin, so her bangles slip. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as the bangles loosening at his departure; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it, saying he had parted in mind while still with her in body, and her bangles knew it first. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa’s exiled Yaksha, pining for his wife, has grown so thin that his golden bracelet has slipped from his wasted forearm.
hinduism.explanation: The slipping bracelet is a classical Indian sign of a body wasted by separation from the beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same sign, bangles loosened by grief, to show separation felt in the body.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s famous opening image; the bracelet slipping from a love-wasted arm is a near-exact parallel, though here it is the husband who wastes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh”
christianity.explanation: The bride’s heart registers her beloved’s presence even while she sleeps.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly has something other than the conscious mind, her bangles, register the beloved’s absence first.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); matches awareness of the beloved below conscious thought, but it senses his arrival, not his parting.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when the caravan departed [from Egypt], their father said, ‘Indeed, I find the smell of Joseph [and would say that he was alive] if you did not think me weakened in mind.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob senses Joseph before any news of him arrives.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s bangles, Jacob perceives the truth about his beloved before anyone tells him.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a good match on sensing ahead of knowing, though it concerns a son’s return, not a spouse’s departure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke.”
judaism.explanation: The bride discovers too late that her beloved has already withdrawn.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, too, realises only after the fact that her beloved had already turned away.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good match on discovering a beloved’s withdrawal, though without the bangle sign.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When a deva is about to pass away from the company of devas, five omens appear: his garlands wither, his clothes get soiled, sweat comes out of his armpits, a dullness descends on his body, he no longer delights in his own deva-seat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Itivuttaka lists bodily omens that announce a coming departure before it happens.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s slipping bangles are such an omen: the body’s adornments signal a parting before the mind admits it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the motif of ornaments and body signalling departure, but the departure is a deva’s death, not a lover’s leaving.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the famous man presented the charioteer with his pair of earrings, his neck-chain, and all his ornaments.”
jainism.explanation: Arishtanemi’s giving away his ornaments is the first outward sign that he is about to leave his bride for the ascetic life.
jainism.tie_back: In the Kural the slipping bangles mark a separation; in the Jain story the removed ornaments mark a groom’s departure from his bride.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial parallel of ornaments signalling separation, but it is the departing groom, not the grieving bride, whose ornaments go.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Dido senses Aeneas’s secret preparations to sail before he tells her, for, as Virgil asks, who can deceive a lover?
greek_mythology.explanation: Virgil shows a lover perceiving her beloved’s intent to leave before any word is spoken.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife, like Dido, knows of the parting before being told, through her bangles.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line (‘quis fallere possit amantem?’); a strong match on a lover sensing a hidden departure, though Aeneid is Roman rather than Greek.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal holds that the heart perceives some truths before and apart from reasoning.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural gives the same priority to a non-rational knowing, voiced through her bangles before her mind.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; paraphrase; cf. tr. W.F. Trotter)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim; a fair match on knowing before reason does, though Pascal speaks of faith rather than separation.

kurals.tamil:
நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார்எம் காதலர் யாமும்
எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Nerunatruch chendraarem kaadhalar yaamum
ezhunaalem meni pasandhu.
kurals.meaning: My beloved left only yesterday, yet my body has grown pale as though seven days had passed.
kurals.elementary: When someone you love goes away, even one day can feel like a whole week. The heroine says her husband left just yesterday, but she already looks as tired and pale as if he had been gone seven days.
kurals.university: The wife tells her confidante that her kātalar (beloved) left only neṟunaṟṟu (yesterday), yet she is like one parted for eḻu nāḷ (seven days), her mēṉi (body, complexion) pacantu, turned pale with pacalai, the sallow pallor that classical Tamil love poetry treats as the visible sign of separation. All four commentators on both sites agree on the sense; Kalaignar loosens ‘seven days’ to ‘many days’. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The pallor here is itself one of the chapter’s ‘signs’, read on the body rather than in speech.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gopi Gita the cowherd women tell Krishna that when they cannot see him even a fraction of a second becomes like an age.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis describe how separation from the beloved stretches time beyond measure.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels one day as seven for the same reason.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31.15 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse (‘truṭi yugāyate tvām apaśyatām’); a strong match on separation lengthening time, though it does not mention pallor; live page could not be re-checked this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.”
christianity.explanation: Love made seven years of waiting feel like a few days to Jacob.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural shows the reverse distortion of time by love: one day apart feels like seven.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a striking mirror-image match on love distorting time, even down to the number seven, though in the opposite direction.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s grief at separation from Joseph shows itself physically in his eyes.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural, too, separation from a loved one is written on the body, as pallor.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a good match on grief of separation marking the body, though the love is parental.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My heart is smitten like grass, and withered; for I forget to eat my bread.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes affliction so deep that the body withers and forgets food.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife shows the same bodily withering, as pallor brought on by separation.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); matches distress showing in the body, but the psalm is a prayer in affliction, not love-longing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada observes that suffering stretches time and distance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences exactly that stretching: one day of separation is long as seven.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a good match on suffering lengthening time, though its point is about samsara rather than love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati’s grief at Arishtanemi’s departure shows at once in her lost cheer.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural’s wife turns pale a day after her husband leaves, Rajimati’s brightness leaves her the moment she hears of his going.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a fair match on immediate visible grief at a beloved’s departure, though Rajimati soon turns to renunciation herself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes the symptoms that overcome her at the sight of the beloved: her tongue breaks, fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, and she becomes paler than grass.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho treats love’s turmoil as a set of visible bodily symptoms, including pallor.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s pasalai is the same pallor, read by all as a sign of love.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the famous fragment; a strong match on pallor as love’s sign, though Sappho describes jealousy in the beloved’s presence, not separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine concludes that time is measured in the mind, as the stretching of the soul through memory, attention and expectation.
philosophy.explanation: For Augustine, how long time is depends on the mind that experiences it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife lives this out: her mind stretches one day of absence into seven.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous argument; a partial match on subjective time, though Augustine’s inquiry is metaphysical, not emotional.

kurals.tamil:
தொடிநோக்கி மென்தோளும் நோக்கி அடிநோக்கி
அஃதாண் டவள்செய் தது.
kurals.transliteration:
Thodinokki mendholum nokki adinokki
ahdhaandaval seydhadhu.
kurals.meaning: She looked at her bangles, looked at her soft shoulders, and looked at her feet: that is what she did there.
kurals.elementary: Without saying a word, the girl looks at her bangles, then her arms, then her feet. Her friend explains what she means: ‘If you leave, I will grow thin and my bangles will slip off, so I’d rather walk with you.’ Her looks said it all.
kurals.university: This couplet is a pure kuṟippu: three looks, at her toṭi (bangles), her meṉ tōḷ (soft shoulders) and her aṭi (feet), with the comment ‘that is what she did there’ (aḵtu āṇṭu avaḷ ceytatu). It is traditionally spoken by the confidante to the hero, explaining the heroine’s silent gestures. Varadarasanar and Kesikan identify the sign as uṭaṉpōkku, her resolve to go with him on his journey; Solomon Pappaiah spells out the logic: the bangles will slip and the shoulders waste if he leaves her, and her looking at her feet means she will walk with him. Kalaignar reads it the same way. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, which print the āytam form அஃதாண் டவள்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama is exiled to the forest, Sita refuses to be left behind and insists that a wife’s place is beside her husband, saying she will walk ahead of him through the wilderness.
hinduism.explanation: Sita chooses to share Rama’s hard journey rather than be separated from him.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine’s look at her feet in the Kural signals the same resolve: she will go with him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a strong match on a wife resolving to accompany her husband, though Sita says it in words and the Kural’s heroine only by signs.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:”
christianity.explanation: Ruth refuses to be parted from Naomi and vows to go wherever she goes.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s silent glance at her feet carries Ruth’s spoken vow: where you go, I go.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on resolving to accompany a loved one, though Ruth’s bond is with her mother-in-law.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abraham leaves Hagar and her infant in the barren valley of Mecca, she follows him asking to whom he is leaving them, until he indicates that God commanded it, and she accepts.
islam.explanation: Hagar follows her departing husband and seeks his meaning when he gives no words.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Hagar confronts a husband’s departure; but where she stays by God’s command, the heroine signals she will go.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, not re-verified this session; a partial match on a wife facing her husband’s departure, with the opposite outcome.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I remember for thee the affection of thy youth, the love of thine espousals; how thou wentest after Me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.”
judaism.explanation: God recalls Israel’s early love as a bride who followed her beloved into the wilderness.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s look at her feet promises the same bridal devotion: to follow her husband even into a hard land.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a good match on a bride following her beloved through a wilderness, though the bride is Israel and the beloved God.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Prince Vessantara is banished to the mountains, his wife Maddi refuses to stay behind in comfort and goes with him into the forest with their children.
buddhism.explanation: Maddi chooses hardship beside her husband over safety apart from him.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine of the Kural signals the same choice with a glance at her feet.
buddhism.source: Vessantara Jataka (Jataka 547) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell and W.H.D. Rouse)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous Jataka; a strong match on a wife accompanying her husband into hardship, though the story’s focus is Vessantara’s generosity.

jainism.quote_or_event: After Arishtanemi renounces the world, Rajimati cuts off her hair, takes vows herself, and sets out for Mount Raivataka, where he had gone.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati follows her betrothed, but along the path of renunciation rather than of married life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine resolves to go where her husband goes; Rajimati does too, though her journey is toward liberation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.29-33 (paraphrase of tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against the sacred-texts.com text; a fair match on following the beloved’s path, but reframed as renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Medea leaves her father’s house at night and flees with Jason aboard the Argo rather than be parted from him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius tells of a young woman who chooses to leave home and go with her beloved.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Udanpokku, the heroine’s resolve to go with her lover, is exactly what Medea does.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; matches a woman resolving to go with her lover, though Medea’s flight involves betrayal of her family and violence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine recalls that as an infant he learned what adults meant from their gestures, the movements of the face and eyes and limbs that he calls the natural language of all peoples.
philosophy.explanation: Augustine treats gesture and glance as a language understood before and beneath words.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s three glances are such a natural language, and the confidante reads them perfectly.
philosophy.source: Augustine, Confessions I.8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Pusey)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a good match on meaning conveyed by glances and gestures, though Augustine describes language learning, not love.

kurals.tamil:
பெண்ணினால் பெண்மை உடைத்தென்ப கண்ணினால்
காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Penninaal penmai udaiththenpa kanninaal
kaamanoi solli iravu.
kurals.meaning: They say that to show the pain of love with the eyes and so plead with the beloved is womanliness beyond womanliness.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes the bravest thing a shy person can do is to show with their eyes how much they need someone, without saying it out loud. The poet says that this gentle, silent asking is the finest kind of grace.
kurals.university: The couplet generalises the chapter: kaṇṇiṉāl kāma nōy colli iravu, ‘telling the sickness of love with the eyes and entreating’, is said (eṉpa, ‘they say’) to be peṇmai, womanliness, added to womanliness (peṇṇiṉāl peṇmai uṭaittu). Varadarasanar and Kesikan specify the entreaty as asking the husband not to leave; Kalaignar makes it a plea to be taken along, linking it to 1279’s udanpokku; Solomon Pappaiah frames it as asking that the love-sickness be cured. Pope renders the sense as ‘womanhood’s most womanly device’. The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; its framing assumes the classical ideal that a woman should not declare love in words, which modern readers may note as a convention of its time.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the fourth canto, Radha’s friend goes to Krishna and describes how Radha, wasting with longing, can only show her love-sickness in her sighs and looks, pleading for him to come.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha conveys her love-sickness through signs that her friend interprets to Krishna.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural praises exactly this: love-sickness told without words, as a silent plea.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a reasonable match on wordless love-sickness carried to the beloved, though in the Gita Govinda a friend speaks on Radha’s behalf.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride wants her beloved to know of her love-sickness and sends word through others.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same plea, telling her love-sickness, but with her eyes alone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match on making love-sickness known to the beloved, though by message rather than by glance.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those in need who, out of dignity, do not ask aloud but whose need can be read in their bearing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise honours an entreaty made through signs rather than open asking.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a good structural match on dignified, wordless asking, though the context is poverty, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Esther’s first plea to the king is made simply by standing before him, and he grants her favour before she speaks.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, honours a plea made by presence and look rather than by words.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); matches a silent, effective entreaty, though Esther pleads for her people, not out of love-sickness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As a bee gathers honey from the flower without injuring its color or fragrance, even so the sage goes on his alms-round in the village.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist monk asks for alms only by his quiet presence, taking without burdening the giver.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly honours an asking done gently and wordlessly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; only a loose next-best match on gentle, wordless asking, in a monastic rather than romantic setting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “It will always cause difficulties to a houseless monk to get everything by begging, and nothing without begging.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana counts the need to ask (yacana) among the troubles a monk must bear with dignity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also concerns the dignity of asking, honouring a woman who pleads through her eyes rather than in words.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a weak next-best match on the hardship and dignity of asking, in a monastic context unrelated to love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nausicaa asks her father for a wagon to wash clothes, too shy to mention her hopes of marriage, but he understands everything she leaves unsaid.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows a young woman’s unspoken wish read perfectly by someone who loves her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural praises the same modest, unspoken asking that is nonetheless understood.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.66-67 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong match on a modest, unspoken wish being understood, though it is a father, not a lover, who reads it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Montaigne lists the many things we do with our hands, head, eyes and brows, asking, promising, entreating, refusing, and says they form a language anyone can understand.
philosophy.explanation: Montaigne argues that gestures and looks make up a full, universal language.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s entreaty made with the eyes is a case of this silent language at its most delicate.
philosophy.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays II.12, ‘Apology for Raymond Sebond’ (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a fair match on entreaty by gesture and look, though Montaigne’s purpose is comparing humans and animals.
